explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. The sons of the prophets tell Elisha, "Please take note that the place where we meet with you is too small for us." (2 Kings 6:1) Elisha is a prophet in Israel, and this group meets with him. I know that feeling, because my first bakery counter had room for me, one mixing bowl and a whole lot of elbow bumping.

Noise isn't the problem here. The text says the place where they meet with Elisha is "too small for us." (2 Kings 6:1) Nobody complains about volume. I think a crowded room can get loud, but the verse only mentions the size.
Nobody mentions the weather, friend. The sons of the prophets say the place is "too small for us." (2 Kings 6:1) So the trouble is room, not temperature. Too small, and that's why they want to build.

Right on the money. The sons of the prophets ask to go to the Jordan and get a log each, and Elisha answers with one word: "Go." (2 Kings 6:2) No speech, no list of rules. Just a green light, and a short one.

Elisha doesn't hold them back, friend. After they ask to go to the Jordan, get a log each and build a place to live, he says, "Go." (2 Kings 6:2) That's a yes, and a short one. Some answers don't need extra words.

That's the one. A man says, "Please come with your servants." (2 Kings 6:3) He asks Elisha to walk out there with them. I'd like to think a crew works better when the leader shows up too, but that's just me talking.
Close to something that makes sense, but the text doesn't say that. The man says, "Please come with your servants." (2 Kings 6:3) He asks Elisha to come along. Nobody asks him to choose a spot.
The logs don't come up in this request, friend. The man says, "Please come with your servants." (2 Kings 6:3) He wants Elisha to come with them. That's the whole ask.
Yes, friend. Elisha answers, "I will come." (2 Kings 6:3) Short and sweet, and he doesn't make anybody beg. Verse 4 says Elisha went with them.
Elisha says yes to this one. His answer is, "I will come." (2 Kings 6:3) Then verse 4 says he went with them. So he's right there at the Jordan.

That's what the text says. "As one of them was cutting down a tree, the iron axe head fell into the water." (2 Kings 6:5) One swing and the head is gone. I've dropped a lot of things in my day, but never something into a whole river.

Sadly, it did happen. The text says, "As one of them was cutting down a tree, the iron axe head fell into the water." (2 Kings 6:5) The head came off while he was cutting. That's why the story turns here.

You've got it. He cries out, "Oh, my master, it was borrowed!" (2 Kings 6:5) That one word is the whole worry. Losing your own tool is bad enough, but I think losing someone else's makes your stomach drop.
The text doesn't say that, friend. The man cries out, "Oh, my master, it was borrowed!" (2 Kings 6:5) Nothing is said about it being new. The word that matters is borrowed.
No father shows up in this story. The man cries out, "Oh, my master, it was borrowed!" (2 Kings 6:5) It belonged to somebody else, and the text doesn't say who. So we leave that open.
Right. "Where did it fall?" asks the man of God. (2 Kings 6:6) That's a question about the spot, nothing else. No scolding, no lecture, and I'll admit I'd have had a lot to say.

explanations.answer: Who did you borrow it from
explanations.explanation: Elisha doesn't ask that, friend. His question is, "Where did it fall?" (2 Kings 6:6) He wants the place in the water. The owner's name never comes up.

explanations.answer: How did it slip off the handle
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't have Elisha asking that. He asks, "Where did it fall?" (2 Kings 6:6) He's asking about the place, not what went wrong. And look at that, no blame at all.
Yes, a stick. The man of God "cut a stick, threw it there, and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) Plain wood, nothing fancy. I've got a whole bakery of tools, and I'd never have guessed this one.
No rope in this story, friend. The man of God "cut a stick, threw it there, and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) Elisha cuts a stick, not a rope. A rope would've been my guess too, though.
Not a strap. The text says the man of God "cut a stick, threw it there, and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) He cut it fresh from a tree, right there by the river. The answer is stick.
That's what happens. The man of God threw the stick there "and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) Iron doesn't float, friend, and that's the point. I'll say it again, IRON FLOATED.
The water stays where it is. The text says the man of God threw the stick there "and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) The river doesn't open up. The iron comes up to the top.
It's the other way around, friend. The man of God threw the stick there "and made the iron float." (2 Kings 6:6) The text doesn't say the stick sank. The heavy iron is what floats.
Not quite, friend. Elisha says, "Lift it out," and the man "reached out his hand and took it." (2 Kings 6:7) He doesn't dive anywhere. The iron is already floating, so he just grabs it.
That's right. Elisha says, "Lift it out," and the man "reached out his hand and took it." (2 Kings 6:7) No diving, no swimming, no wet apron. He reaches out and the iron is right there.
